summary: A fixed-frequency transmon qubit demonstrates heralded leakage detection by applying a resonant Rabi drive during dispersive readout, which makes the computational states indistinguishable while preserving distinguishability of higher excited states. The protocol achieves 97.1(3)% leakage-detection fidelity with 2.3(3)% false-flag rate and 92.9(5)% average post-detection state fidelity for equal computational-leakage mixtures, requiring no additional hardware.
motivation: Leakage from the computational subspace is a major error mechanism in superconducting processors that persists over error-correction cycles, and detecting leakage without disturbing quantum information enables heralded error signals for decoders while managing leakage-induced correlated errors.
method: A detuned Rabi drive at $\Omega_q / 2\pi = 186$ MHz on the $|g\rangle$–$|e\rangle$ transition during 80 ns of dispersive readout time-averages the state-dependent cavity pull, making the dressed computational states transparent to the probe while leaving $|f\rangle$ and higher states dispersively coupled and detectable; the optimal detuning $\delta / 2\pi \approx +11$ MHz compensates residual dephasing from finite anharmonicity ($\alpha / 2\pi = -318$ MHz).
result: Binary classification yields $\varepsilon_{FF} = 2.3(3)\%$ false-flag rate and $\varepsilon_{UL} = 3.5(2)\%$ undetected-leakage rate; errors decompose into separation errors $\varepsilon_{sep} \approx 2\%$ and flip errors (0.2% and 1.6% respectively); with narrower filter bandwidth $\kappa_{\mathrm{eff}} / 2\pi \approx |\chi|$, projections suggest false-flag rates below 1% and back-action of $\sim 10^{-3}$ at $10^{-3}$ separation error with current coherence times $T_1 \approx 27$ µs.
